blocks.text: A 50-year-old man walks into the clinic looking thin, slightly yellow in the eyes, with fingertips that bulge like drumsticks. Before you ask a single question, your eyes have already collected clues pointing to the lungs, the liver or the heart. General inspection is the cheapest and often the most informative part of any examination.

blocks.markdown: **General inspection** is the structured observation of the patient from the end of the bed or across the room, followed by close inspection of the **hands**, which often show signs of systemic disease. It is done in good light (preferably natural daylight) with the patient comfortably exposed. Always begin with the **overall impression** and then examine specific signs: clubbing, anaemia, jaundice and cyanosis.

### Describing general appearance

Use a systematic checklist so that nothing is missed:

- **Level of consciousness and orientation**, and whether the patient looks comfortable or **in distress**.
- **Build and nutrition**: thin, cachectic, obese.
- **Posture and movement**: sitting forward, guarding the abdomen, restlessness.
- **Breathing**: rate, effort, use of accessory muscles, audible noises.
- **Skin colour**: pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, flushing.
- **Hydration**: dry mucous membranes, skin turgor.
- **Surroundings**: oxygen, walking aids, medication, sputum pot.

Describe what you see in neutral words ("thin, breathless at rest, sitting upright") rather than labels ("looks terrible").

blocks.title: Clubbing
blocks.text: **Clubbing** is the painless, soft-tissue enlargement of the ends of the fingers (and toes) with loss of the normal angle between the nail and the nail fold (the Lovibond angle, about 160 degrees normally, which becomes 180 degrees or more in clubbing), nail-bed sponginess and increased curvature of the nail.

blocks.caption: Key general signs: what to look for, where, and common associations
rows: Lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease
Inside the lower eyelid (conjunctiva), palmar creases, tongue
Iron deficiency, chronic disease, blood loss, haemolysis
Sclerae (whites of the eyes) in daylight, skin
Liver disease, bile duct obstruction, haemolysis
Severe lung disease, right-to-left cardiac shunt

blocks.markdown:
### Anaemia, jaundice and cyanosis

**Anaemia.** Pull down the lower eyelid gently and look at the conjunctiva: it should be pink. Pale conjunctivae and pale palmar creases suggest a low haemoglobin, though pallor is an unreliable sign and cannot replace a blood test.

**Jaundice.** Yellow discolouration of the sclerae and skin caused by raised bilirubin; it is usually first visible in the sclerae when the serum bilirubin rises above roughly 40 micromoles per litre (about 2.5 mg/dL); the exact threshold varies. Look in daylight, because artificial light can mimic or hide jaundice.

**Cyanosis.** A blue tinge of skin and mucous membranes. **Central** cyanosis (tongue, lips) reflects poorly oxygenated arterial blood; **peripheral** cyanosis (fingers, toes) can occur with a normal arterial oxygen content, for example from cold. Cyanosis becomes visible when the concentration of **deoxygenated haemoglobin exceeds about 5 g/dL**.

blocks.caption: [Hb] is total haemoglobin in g/dL and S_aO2 is arterial oxygen saturation expressed as a fraction.

blocks.title: Why an anaemic patient may not look blue
blocks.prompt: A patient has haemoglobin 8 g/dL and an arterial oxygen saturation of 75% (0.75). Is central cyanosis likely to be visible?

steps.text: Compare with the visibility threshold of about 5 g/dL: 2.0 g/dL is well below it.
Conclusion: this patient is badly hypoxaemic but is unlikely to look cyanosed because there is too little haemoglobin to produce the blue colour.

blocks.answer: Deoxyhaemoglobin is about 2 g/dL, below the cyanosis threshold, so cyanosis is unlikely to be visible despite hypoxaemia.

blocks.markdown:
### Examining the hands

The hands offer many clues. Look at the **nails**, the **palms** and the **backs** of the hands, then feel the pulse and check for **tremor** and **flapping**.

- **Cardiovascular**: clubbing, **splinter haemorrhages** (thin dark lines under the nail, as in infective endocarditis but also from trauma), Osler nodes and Janeway lesions, xanthomata of the tendons.
- **Respiratory**: clubbing, **tar staining** of the fingers (smoking), peripheral cyanosis, and **flapping tremor** due to carbon dioxide retention.
- **Hepatic**: **palmar erythema**, **leukonychia** (white nails, associated with low albumin), **Dupuytren's contracture** (thickening and shortening of the palmar fascia), clubbing, and the **flapping tremor (asterixis)** of hepatic encephalopathy.

blocks.title: Linking signs to a system
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old woman has clubbing, tar-stained fingers and a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. Which system do these findings point toward?

steps.text: Group the findings: clubbing and tar staining and flapping tremor are commonly listed under respiratory disease.
Link each to a mechanism: tar staining points to smoking; clubbing points to chronic lung conditions such as cancer or bronchiectasis; a flapping tremor can occur with carbon dioxide retention.
Avoid certainty: clubbing and flapping tremor also occur with liver disease, so correlate with history and further examination.

blocks.answer: The respiratory system, as the leading consideration, with liver disease kept in mind.

blocks.title: Signs point; they do not prove
blocks.text: Hand and eye signs generate hypotheses. A single sign, such as a splinter haemorrhage, can be benign. Always combine with the history, vital signs and system examination.

items: Inspect from the end of the bed before touching the patient.
Check conjunctivae gently with the lower eyelid pulled down.
Look at both hands, front and back, including the nails.
Describe findings in neutral words and say which system they suggest.

points: General inspection systematically describes consciousness, distress, build, posture, breathing, skin colour and hydration.
Clubbing, pallor, jaundice and cyanosis are recognised by their location and cause; jaundice is best seen in the sclerae in daylight and central cyanosis in the tongue.
Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of deoxygenated haemoglobin (about 5 g/dL), so anaemic patients may be hypoxaemic without looking blue.
The hands give clues to cardiovascular, respiratory and hepatic disease, but each sign must be correlated with the whole picture.

questions.stem: Where is central cyanosis best seen?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: warm mucous membranes reflect central oxygenation.
distractorRationale.b: Fingertips show peripheral cyanosis, which may occur with cold.
distractorRationale.c: Ankles are not a standard site.
distractorRationale.d: Palms are used for pallor and erythema.

questions.explanation: Central cyanosis reflects poorly oxygenated arterial blood and is seen in warm mucous membranes such as the tongue. Peripheral cyanosis in the fingers can be caused by cold alone.

questions.stem: Which feature is the best site to examine for jaundice in a 48-year-old man?

options.text: The soles of the feet, in dim light
The nail beds under fluorescent light

distractorRationale.a: Correct: jaundice is first seen in the sclerae.
distractorRationale.d: Conjunctival pallor is for anaemia, and the sclera is the more specific site for yellow.

questions.explanation: Bilirubin binds to the elastin-rich sclerae, so they become yellow early. Natural daylight gives the most reliable colour assessment.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has loss of the angle between the nail and nail fold in all fingers, with spongy nail beds and curved nails. This is best described as:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of nail-fold angle, sponginess and increased curvature.
distractorRationale.b: Koilonychia is spoon-shaped nails, seen in iron deficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Splinter haemorrhages are thin dark lines under the nail.

questions.explanation: Clubbing is defined by loss of the normal nail-fold angle together with soft tissue swelling at the nail base. It is associated with a range of lung, heart, liver and bowel diseases.

questions.stem: Which finding on the hands is most associated with chronic liver disease?

distractorRationale.c: Heberden's nodes are osteoarthritic nodules of the distal finger joints.
distractorRationale.d: Raynaud's phenomenon is a vascular response to cold.

questions.explanation: Palmar erythema, leukonychia and Dupuytren's contracture are classic hepatic hand signs. Tar staining points to smoking and therefore to respiratory and cardiovascular risk.

questions.stem: A student notes a single thin dark line under one fingernail in a 30-year-old carpenter who has no fever or murmur. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: It may be a splinter haemorrhage from trauma, and needs correlation before any conclusion
It is a normal feature of clubbing

questions.correctOptionText: It may be a splinter haemorrhage from trauma, and needs correlation before any conclusion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: splinter haemorrhages occur with trauma and are not specific.
distractorRationale.b: One lesion without other features does not prove endocarditis.
distractorRationale.c: Not a sign of liver failure.
distractorRationale.d: Clubbing involves nail angle, not dark lines.

questions.explanation: Isolated splinter haemorrhages are common after trauma, particularly in manual workers. They suggest endocarditis only when multiple and combined with other features.

questions.stem: True or false: pale lower-eyelid conjunctivae in a patient prove that the haemoglobin is low.
questions.explanation: Conjunctival pallor suggests anaemia but is an imprecise sign that can be missed or overcalled. A blood test is needed to confirm anaemia.

questions.stem: A patient with polycythaemia has haemoglobin 20 g/dL and an arterial oxygen saturation of 80%. Calculate the concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin in g/dL, using the lesson formula.
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated haemoglobin equals haemoglobin times the unsaturated fraction: 20 x (1 - 0.80) = 4.0 g/dL. This is close to, but below, the visible cyanosis threshold of about 5 g/dL, so cyanosis would be borderline.

questions.stem: Describe how you would perform a systematic general inspection of a 64-year-old man who has just been admitted to the ward, and state what each observation could tell you.
markingGuide: Introduces self, consent, good lighting and adequate exposure
Alertness and orientation
Distress or comfort at rest
Build and nutritional status
Posture and movement
Breathing pattern and effort
Skin colour: pallor, jaundice, cyanosis
Hydration and surroundings such as oxygen or aids
Uses neutral descriptive words
questions.explanation: General inspection is organised to avoid omissions. Good answers pair each observation with its clinical significance rather than just listing it.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has clubbing and a flapping tremor. Explain the signs you would look for in the hands to help decide whether the problem is cardiovascular, respiratory or hepatic.
markingGuide: Cardiovascular: splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, xanthomata, clubbing
Respiratory: tar staining, clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, CO2 retention flap
Hepatic: palmar erythema, leukonychia, Dupuytren's contracture, asterixis, clubbing
Recognises that some signs overlap (clubbing, flapping tremor)
Signs are correlated with history and the rest of the examination
questions.explanation: The hands offer specific as well as non-specific signs. A strong answer shows that overlapping signs require correlation rather than a firm conclusion.

questions.stem: Explain why a patient with anaemia and hypoxaemia may not appear cyanosed, using the concept of deoxygenated haemoglobin.
markingGuide: Cyanosis depends on the absolute concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin
The visible threshold is about 5 g/dL
Deoxy-Hb = Hb x (1 - saturation)
Low total haemoglobin gives a small absolute amount of deoxygenated haemoglobin
Worked or stated example with numbers
Therefore absence of cyanosis does not exclude hypoxaemia
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is determined by how much deoxygenated haemoglobin there is, not by the percentage saturation alone. A low total haemoglobin can keep that amount below the threshold even when saturation is low.
